Following the adoption of the agreements, some experts13 have introduced the concept of the “Arctic Council System”, which contains two components: The first consists of the Constitutive Declaration, the Ministerial Declarations, any adopted normative instruments (guidelines) and the institutional structure of the Council; while the second comprises tools negotiated under the auspices of the Council and its institutional components.

It is therefore important to highlight that two new platforms for regional cooperation have been established through the work of the AC: The Arctic Economic Council and the Arctic Coast Guard Forum, although the latter is not formally affiliated with the Council. Moreover, at the 2021 Reykjavik Ministerial Meeting the Council approved its first strategic plan with detailed goals and actions to be achieved by 2030 with the aim of making the Council more vigorous by increasing its planning and implementation capacity. Overall, the Arctic Council has maintained a firm position of being equally committed to sustainable development, despite an initial prioritization of environmental protection. In that sense, it focuses on issues related to economic development, education, health and culture of the residents of the High North, among others. In time, the Council managed to internationalize the Arctic problems with the elaboration of high-quality reports and, especially, after the admission of new Observers. The only major disadvantage is that even issues related to soft security (environmental, human, energy security, etc.) are not sufficiently discussed within the AC. Discussions on military security also remain excluded. Therefore, it can be concluded that the Council tries to identify changes in State activities and make them more predictable in order to soften and clarify positions and to ensure that there is no misunderstanding between interested parties. The Spill-Over Effect of the Russian War in Ukraine As already noted, during the Cold War, the perceptions of security in the Arctic were focused on the balance between the two superpowers14. Nowadays, this understanding has expanded to contemporary security aspects that differ according to the object at risk: Human, cultural, energy, economic and environmental security15. It can be argued that since the collapse of the Soviet Union, the order in the High North has been built on three pillars: Favouring the role and interests of the States; highlighting the Council as the leading forum for regional cooperation; and limiting the role of NATO16. The Council indeed emerged as the most prominent actor involved in the governance of the High North, being the only one that embraces all eight Arctic States by providing a forum for discussion of common issues and mediation between them. It can even be argued that using its soft power influence as an integrative force, the long-term aim of the AC has always been to establish political thinking based on win-win strategies of mutual benefit for all, rather than achieving their particular interest17. And indeed, throughout the existence of the Council, no significant sources of discord have been recorded18. However, the ongoing Russian aggression in Ukraine marked the return of geopolitics in the Arctic. This will undoubtedly have a long-term impact on security and cooperation and will seriously hamper the dialogue and open relations between the Russian Federation and its Western partners in the North Polar Region for the years to come. As a matter of fact, even the 2014 Crimea crisis and the deteriorated relations between Russia and the West as a result of the restrictive measures adopted in consequence are an excellent example of how a non-Arctic event can impact cooperation and security in the North Polar Region by increasing the mistrust between the Arctic stakeholders. The 2014 Crimea annexation was followed by political and economic sanctions that affected the Russian oil industry, as Western investments, technologies and expertise for oil and gas extraction in difficult climatic conditions were cancelled. Canada was the first to introduce sanctions against Russia as a warning that aggressive actions would not be accepted within the Arctic space. The cautious stance of the other Arctic States, however, was not able to prevent the freezing of regional political dialogue at the time: Russia was absent from the 2015 Iqaluit Ministerial Meeting, while several coordinated actions were suspended (such as the NORTHERN EAGLE naval exercise between Norway, Russia and the US) and the Arctic Security Forces Roundtable was also held without Russian participation.

Conclusion Over the last decades, the balance of power from the Cold War period has been fading, yielding to strategic interdependence in the High North. The Arctic Council has established itself as the most outstanding actor for regional governance with unquestionable political relevance. Therefore, its future remains a central issue in circumpolar policies as it should become a body that can facilitate policy response to pressing regional challenges.
